title: Piecewise parametric structure in the pooling problem: from sparse strongly-polynomial solutions to NP-hardness
contribution: Parametrising single-quality standard pooling by pool concentration exposes sparse dominant active topologies and a piecewise objective, giving strongly-polynomial algorithms for I+H-1-1, I+H-1-J and I+H-L-1 subclasses (Haverly instances included) and a new P/NP boundary point.
problem_entry: Global solvers stall on large pooling instances while simple piecewise-linear/MILP approaches work in practice; the paper sets out to validate Floudas' piecewise intuition and close a P/NP gap left by Alfaki-Haugland, with direct feeds added (pp. 1-2, 4, 27).
key_idea: Keep pool concentration p as a parameter: for fixed p the problem is an LP with a tiny optimal basis, so active sets, dominance relations and breakpoints describe f*(p) as piecewise linear/constant/monotone convex-concave; extend by additive decomposition over outputs and at most two active pools (pp. 7-12, 20-25, 29).
assumptions: Assumption 2.2: single quality, feasible, feed availability and pool capacity dropped, fixed demands D_j>0; authors show it is tight (relaxing it erodes sparsity or gives NP-hardness); rational data for Thm 4.4 (pp. 5-6, 22, 25, 27-28).
proof_devices: Geometric contradiction: quadrilateral i-l-j-k shows breakpoints only at input concentrations (Thm 3.1.6, Fig. 3, pp. 11-12)
Joint-node aggregation of an active pair with averaged cost gamma_ij(p) (Def 3.1.3, p. 10)
Reduction by analogy: directs-only mirrors inputs-only with p replaced by quality bound P(i,j) (Prop 3.2.4, Cors 3.2.5-3.2.6, pp. 14-15, 32)
Pre-solve inputs, then treat the joint input node as an extra direct (Thm 3.3.1, pp. 16-17)
Closed-form n-th derivatives give monotone convex/concave pieces (Prop 3.3.7, pp. 20, 34)
Additive decomposition over outputs linked by p (Thm 4.1, pp. 23-25)
Small constructed counterexamples for non-monotonicity and multimodality (Prop 4.3, p. 25)
Stationary points via LLL factorisation of a rational univariate polynomial (Thm 4.4, p. 26)
Hardness frontier: each relaxation of Assumption 2.2 maps to an NP-hard polynomial system (Remark 4.6, pp. 27-28)
experiments: No benchmark; four constructed numerical illustrations (Figs 4, 6, 8, 10, pp. 12, 21, 27, 31) and code released on GitHub (p. 3, ref [8] p. 34).
positioning: Unifies and generalises Boland et al. |K|=1 complexity results, fills Alfaki-Haugland gap, credits Beale et al., Meyer-Floudas, Karuppiah-Grossmann and Dey-Gupte without criticism; links pooling to queueing (pp. 2, 27-28, 32).
writing: Roadmap paragraph before each section, theorem-dense with a worked figure after each structural result, rare exclamation marks for surprises (Haverly), intuition credited to named predecessors (pp. 2, 9, 13, 28, 32).
limits_future: Sparsity and analytic solvability vanish once flow bounds, multiple qualities or variable demands return (NP-hard); future: approximation algorithms from the boundary subclass and disjunctive cuts on the identified structures (pp. 22, 27-28, 31-32).

method_links.note: Structure as insider information found analytically: sparse dominant active topologies and piecewise objective, exploited for exact solution (not a software detector).
Audits a classic benchmark family by theory: the Haverly instances, used for 35+ years to test exponential algorithms, lie in a strongly-polynomial subclass.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Fix the bilinear-coupling variable as a parameter, bound LP basis cardinality, enumerate dominance breakpoints to describe the optimum over the parameter.
Each relaxation of Assumption 2.2 is shown to erode sparsity or yield NP-hardness, turning a convenience assumption into a mapped P/NP boundary.

transferable: Keep the complicating variable of a bilinear model as a parameter and characterise the optimal LP basis as a function of it (pp. 7-12).
Climb a ladder of subclasses and reuse each result as a building block (pp. 3, 6, 22-23, 28-29).
Justify a restrictive assumption by showing every relaxation of it is NP-hard (pp. 22, 27-28, 31).
Check whether a classic benchmark family lies in an easy subclass before using it to evaluate exponential algorithms (p. 28).

quotes.text: The proofs lead to the unexpected outcome that the famous Haverly [33] pooling instances, i.e. the first-recorded pooling instances, belong to a strongly-polynomial subclass!
The position on the P/NP boundary of the multiple outputs and one pool subclass is thus an ideal starting point for approximating algorithms that cross into NP-hardness.

title: Designing and implementing algorithms for mixedinteger nonlinear optimization
contribution: Edited Dagstuhl 18081 report setting a MINLP research agenda: solver needs analysis, MIP/NLP/application/ML connections, sound-experimentation recommendations (permuted models, informative output, MINLP kappa, no simplistic comparisons) and open problems; includes her group's NN-selected SDP-cut and gradient-boosted-tree abstracts.
problem_entry: Mismatch between natural models for important problems and solvers that often cannot solve practically-sized instances; obstacles named as computability boundary, exploiting specialised classes and holistic use of logic (p. 1).
key_idea: Bring theory and implementation experts, MIP and NLP communities, application experts and ML together; her group contributes offline NN selection of strong linear cuts from SDP relaxations (pp. 6-7) and exact B&B plus heuristics over gradient-boosted trees on a BASF instance (p. 17).
assumptions: n/a (seminar report); §3.3 assumes nonconvex continuous QP with SDP relaxations, §3.26 trained gradient-boosted trees (pp. 6, 17).
experiments: none reported; the experimentation working group recommends permuted-model runs, richer solver output, a MINLP kappa analogue and no simplistic comparisons, and a new metric set is announced but not given (pp. 2, 21-22).
positioning: MINLP as superset of MIP and NLP that should become as ubiquitous as they are; energy group says the mathematical community may overemphasise proving optimality versus quick robust near-optimal answers (pp. 1-2, 21).
writing: Agenda prose with bullet-list conclusions and open questions; promises a special issue and an open-problem paper (pp. 2, 22-23).
limits_future: No data; promised metrics and open-problem document only announced; open problems on column generation, SOC-representability, sub-solver reliability, extended formulations; growth areas ML, OPF, pooling (pp. 2, 23).

method_links.note: Joint editorial voice: permuted-model experiments, informative output, numerical-safety measure, distrust of simplistic comparisons (SKILL U7 notes later non-adherence).
Early form of trees-as-constraints: partner's GBT catalyst model, heuristics plus structure-exploiting exact B&B, BASF industrial instance, 'risk control' still in title.
Executive summary celebrates new solver-comparison metrics made at the seminar, a community-made counterpart to Warning sign 2 (self-invented metric).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: NN estimator trained before solver installation selects few strong low-dimensional linear cuts that retain SDP tightness (the SKILL's U5 line; no results given here).

transferable: Benchmark MINLP solvers on permuted copies of each model, vary tolerances and report variability rather than single runs (p. 22; p. 20).
Move an expensive per-node selection step offline into an estimator trained before deployment (pp. 6-7).
coauthors: Pierre Bonami, Ambros M. Gleixner, Jeff Linderoth (co-editors); edited in cooperation with Radu Baltean-Lugojan

quotes.text: the need to incorporate experimentation on permuted models as has become standard in the MIP community;
Finally, a new set of metrics for comparing MINLP solvers were developed at this meeting and will greatly aid future solver testing.

title: QPLIB: a library of quadratic programming instances
contribution: First comprehensive QP/MIQCQP instance library (453 instances filtered from >8000) with an OVC taxonomy, solver-portfolio difficulty filtering, unreformulated instances, public metadata website and a new .qplib format; deliberately no solver comparison.
problem_entry: No single library covered all kinds of QP instances; existing ones were application- or structure-specific; the challenge is choosing a set neither onerous nor easy for very different communities (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Define 'interesting' as challenging for a significant set of solution methods, select via a containment-ordered three-field taxonomy and two cascaded filters, keep instances in the contributor's natural form (pp. 2, 6-8, 15-16).
assumptions: Convexity marked only by the sufficient (definiteness) condition with eigenvalue threshold 1e-12, so SOC-as-quadratic counts as potentially nonconvex; Neumaier's incomplete/asymptotically complete/complete/rigorous solver classes; Turing machine vs Real RAM caveat on 'exact' (pp. 6, 8, 10-13, 15).
experiments: Library-construction protocol: Jan 2014 call open ten months plus seven libraries gave >8000 instances in GAMS; filter 1 drops instances solved by >=30% of complete solvers in 30 s; filter 2 deduplicates by donor/size and drops anything a complete QGQ solver solves in 120 s; 319 discrete + 134 continuous; feature plots; no performance data by design (pp. 13-20).
positioning: Modelled on MIPLIB and MINLPLib 2 tooling; QP as sweet spot between MILP and MINLP and meeting ground of combinatorial and nonlinear communities; performance delegated to Mittelmann benchmarks (pp. 1-4, 14, 20).
writing: Repeated explicit disclaimers of what the paper does not do (no solver comparison) and choices justified as avoiding solver bias; closes calling the library a snapshot to be extended (pp. 2, 4, 8, 21).
limits_future: Snapshot of past problem types; coarse taxonomy omits finer structures; convexity under-detected; plans literature references on website and dynamic extension (pp. 8, 10, 21).

method_links.note: Joint voice: largest documented collection with provenance, explicit solver-portfolio difficulty thresholds, public metadata and formats.
Calibration aims at instances few complete solvers solve quickly, not Heuristic 3's 'baseline wins some'.
Library deliberately does not detect hidden convex structure (SOC as quadratic), leaving detection to solvers because only some detect it.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Instances kept if few complete solvers solve them quickly; drop thresholds 30% of solvers / 30 s and one complete solver / 120 s.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: keep instances in natural form to avoid solver bias
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: No reformulation, since reformulations favour one solver class.

transferable: Two-stage benchmark filter: drop instances that >=X% of complete solvers solve in T s, then deduplicate by donor/size and drop those a strong solver solves in a longer limit; report counts per stage (pp. 15-16).
Classify each instance with a containment-ordered code computed from data and publish raw features as downloadable metadata (pp. 6, 14-15, 20-21).
State the complete-vs-rigorous and Turing-machine-vs-Real-RAM caveat when calling floating-point global solvers exact (pp. 10, 12-13).
coauthors: F. Furini, E. Traversi, P. Belotti, A. Frangioni, A. Gleixner, N. Gould, L. Liberti, A. Lodi, H. Mittelmann, N. Sahinidis, S. Vigerske, A. Wiegele

quotes.text: Thanks to these extensive preliminary tests, we discarded all instances that are solved by at least 30% of the complete solvers within a time limit of 30 seconds.
This being a bias that we do not want to add we have chosen to keep the instances in their “natural” form, this being the one in which the original contributor initially wrote them.
